newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS -Hungary to decide on anti-inflation plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -Hungary to decide on anti-inflation plan.

text.p: Hungary's government is likely to discuss within three weeks two alternative programmes of reducing inflation in 1998, Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy told Reuters in an interview on Monday.
"This is a matter of such importance that before (the government discussion) I will ask the Prime Minister and the central bank president for a joint consultation," he said.
Medgyessy declined to disclose details of the plans, but said that under an optimal scenario envisaged by one of the programmes year-on-year price growth would fall below 10 percent in December 1998.
The alternative proposal would see inflation of up to three percentage points higher. He also said that the more radical cut would be better for growth.

"The chance of that (larger inflation reduction) depends very much on what the social partners (employers and trade unions) are ready to accept and what parts of the anti-inflationary programme politicians are willing to undertake," he said.
He said that year-on-year inflation could go down to between 16 to 17 percent by December 1997 from 18.8 percent in March, adding that he would be able to give a more precise forecast in June.
Medgyessy said the ministry maintained its 18 percent average inflation forecast for 1997, compared with an average inflation of 23.6 percent last year.
He said the government's approval for a draft pension reform last week showed that it did not hesitate to make decisions for the long-term even though 1998 elections were near.
"I think the government will be able to undertake the programme (including the larger inflation cut) despite the difficult situation," he said.
"I would rather ask whether the necessary confidence of the social partners can be created," he said. "I think that if they see guarantees, they will agree."

Whichever of the two programmes is approved, government intervention would use only tools which are usual in market economies, such as decisions on interest and exchange rates, the reserve requirement and money market interventions, Medgyessy said.
He said that declining inflation and structural reforms would support increasing and sustainable economic growth.

Hungary targets a gross domestic product (GDP) growth of two to three percent this year, up from a preliminary figure of one percent in 1996, and plans to boost growth to up to five percent annually in the next few years.
Deep structural reforms, such as overhauling the pensions, should help avoid trade and current account problems which could arise from rising economic growth, Medgyessy said.
He said Hungary's tight austerity policies introduced two years ago were necessary to create conditions for sustainable growth, but alone were not sufficient to sustain it.
He added that the government's pension plan also outlined measures to reform the health care system, but that any concrete moves in this are would come only after the 1998 elections.
